FOREWORD This Indian Standard was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Food Analysis and Nutrition Sectional Committee had been approved by the Food and Agriculture Division Council. Paneer and Chhana are Indian varieties of fresh cheese, the former being used in cooked vegetable dishes and other culinary items, whereas the latter for preparation of certain sweets. Selection of these products for their respective use is greatly influenced by their sensory attributes. This standard is complementarytoIS5162 `Specification for Paneer'. :1980 `Specification for Chhana @-st revision)' and IS 10484:1983

For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2: 1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values (revised)'. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

Indian Standard METHOD FOR SENSORY EVALUATION OF PANEER/CHHAN.A "
1 SCOPE This standard prescribes conditions, technique, method and evaluating card for sensory evaluation of Paneerl Chhana 2 REFERENCES The following standards contain provisions which through reference in this text, constitute provisions of this standard. At the time of publication, the editions indicated were valid. Al} standards are subject to revision, and parties to agreements based on this standard are encouraged to investigate the possibility of applying the most recent editions of the standards indicated below: IS No. 5126 (Part 1): 1969 (Part 2): 1969 6273 (Part 1): 1971 (Part 2): 1971 Title Glossary of general terms for sensory evaluation of foods Methodology Quality characteristics Guide for sensory evaluation of foods Optimum requirements Methods and evaluation of cards the upper and lower molars during mastication. 3.6 Unclean/Utensil-- An unpleasant odour indicative of unclean utensils; the product leaves a distinct aftertaste. 4 GENERAL CONDITIONS

The general conditions for sensory evaluation of Paneer/CMuzna shall be as given in IS 6273 (Part 1). 5 PANELISTS 5.1 Selection Persons with normal sensitivity for taste and odour should be selected. They should have ability to detect small differences between paired samples with minor flavour, colour or textural differences. They should be able to recognize the primary stimuli like sweet, sour, salty and bitter. Selection among the available panelists should be based on their significant capacity to distinguish quality variations and other attributes. Those who dislike Paneer/CWzana or any other milk products should not be included in the panel. 5.2 Training 5.2.1 Preparation of Paneer/Chhana Samples

3 TERMINOLOGY 3.0 For the purpose of this standard, the following definitions in addition to those giveninIS5126 (Part 1) and IS 5126 (Part 2) shall apply. 3.1 Dull -- This appearance defect is indicative dead, unattractive surface look. of a

A control sample of fresh Paneer/Chhana (prepared under standard condition from fresh milk ingredients) representing desirable characteristics like flavour, body and texture, colour and appearance should be served alongwith the sample having one or more of the following defects in different intensities. 5.2.1.1 Acid/sour

3.2 Dry Surface/Surface Skin -- Suggestive for lacking in the desired moistness on the surface. It may be caused by compositional variations or exposure to open air or hot environment. 3.3 FeedlWeed -- Typical of aromatic feeds such as onion and silage and milk tainting weeds consumed by milk animals. Easily detectable by smelling. 3.4 Open -- Openness in texture, particularly undesirable in Paneer is recognized visibly by presence of small voids or absence of a close knit appearance in the cut surface of a product sample. 3.5 Rubbery/Chewy -- A body defect characterized by initial resistance to pressing and subsequent tendency to spring back upon releasing the pressure, as felt between the thumb and the forefinger or between 1

Such a sample can be obtained by employing lower than normal pH (5 or below) for coagulation of milk; vary the moisture retention in such samples to attain different degrees of the defect. 5.2.1.2 Bitter

Prepare Paneer/Chhana from milk having induced rancidity (as, for example by homogenizing raw milk). Incorporation of minute quantities of quinine sulphate during sample preparation would also yield a bitter product. 5.2.1.3 Fat Use milk with 2.0 percent Chhana-making. or less fat for Paneer/

5.3 Number of Paneliits at ordinary temperatures Five to seven panelists should be employed in the evaluation to arrive at consistent and statistically valid results. At least 10 judgments should be taken. 6 SAMPLING, PRESENTATION 6.1 Sampling A representative sample should be drawn from the lot. Precaution should be taken to avoid undue contamination during drawing, handling and presentation of samples. 6.2 Preparation of Samples PREPARATION AND

Hold fresh sample in worm, humid condition for few days. 5.2.1.6 Rancid As in 5.2.1.2. Also the samples obtained in 5.2.1.5 may have bitterness. 5.2.1.7 Stale Extensive holding of good samples at refrigeration temperature would make staleness evident provided that care is taken to avoid excessive fimgal growth. 5.2.1.8 Yeasty Store fresh samples, exposed to atmosphere, at a low temperature for relatively long time. Alternatively, a yeast culture may be used. 5.2.1.9 Hard Hard body may be simulated in Paneer/Chhana by employing more intense pressing, adding calcium chloride to milk prior to coagulation and by using lowfat milk. 5.2.1.10 Pasly Add starch or a gum before coagulating a high moisture product. 5.2.1.11 Rubbe@chewy As in 5.2.1.9. 5.2.1.12 Soji Use of high fat milk and high pH or low temperature for coagulation, and reduce whey drainage during Paneer/Chhana preparation. 5.2.2 Procedure for Training 5.2.2.1 The panelists should be familiarized with all the desirable characteristics of fresh Paneer/Chhana. They should be trained to distinguish between normal and abnormal sensory attributes of Paneer/Chhana and also to recognize the degree of defects. 5.2.2.2 A series of 20 judgments should be obtained from each prospective panelist utilizing a pair of samples with known differences. To compensate for the known variations from day-to-day a quali~ing test is given for a 3-day period. Those who make an acceptable (75 percent correct score should be chosen). 5.2.2.3 The panelists should be checked once in three months for their consistency and acuity. milk to obtain

PaneerlChhana samples should be tempered at 15�20�C for enough time to ensure ideal sample status for sensory evaluation. Samples cut into suitable size pieces should be presented in a large covered petri plate. 6.3 Amount of Each Sample About 25 g of the representative sample should be sufficient. 6.4 Number of Samples Number of samples in one sessiow should not exceed five. 6.5 Coding Coding of samples should be done as recommended under 7 of IS 6273 (Part 1). 7 PROCEDURE 7.1 Technique of Evaluation

Evaluate the package for possible damage, greasiness or soiling. To begin with, note the colour and appearance of the sample. Examine if any visible dird foreign matter is present. Observe the uncut surface more closely for drying, skin or slime formation and moukliness. Note openness, if any. Then feel how the sample responds to pressing by a finger and between the thumb and the forefinger to ascertain its textural properties. Break or cut the sample and pass it slowly under the nose to record its aroma. Try to work a small piece between fingers. Finally take enough of the sample into the mouth and chew it up to a semi-solid state. Observe the sample flavour and textural characteristics as it is being masticated. Note if the sample leaves any afler-taste. 7.2 Method Follow composite scoring method as described in 4.2.8 of IS 6273 (Part 2). 2
